topic_title: Top 13 Calm Dog Breeds Perfect for Quiet Homes
intro: A calm dog is mostly about energy and voice. Low-energy breeds are content with a couple of short walks and long naps, and low-barking breeds keep a home and its neighbors quiet. Watch the trade-offs that often come with calm breeds: giant dogs drool and have short lifespans, flat-faced breeds struggle in heat, and some calm hounds howl. Every puppy is energetic for its first year, so an adult dog is the surest way to get calm from day one.

picks.description: The Japanese Chin is the calmest and quietest pick on this list. It weighs 7 to 11 pounds, needs only short daily walks and indoor play, and rarely barks. Chins are gentle, affectionate and good with children, cats and other dogs, and they are fastidious, often grooming themselves like cats. The silky coat sheds moderately but rarely mats with a brushing once or twice a week. Their flat face makes them sensitive to heat and strenuous exercise. They are reserved with strangers and happiest in a peaceful home.
picks.best_for: Quiet homes and apartments wanting a gentle, small lap dog
picks.quirky_fact: Japanese Chins sometimes spin in circles when excited, a move owners call the Chin spin.
picks.skip_if: You want an outdoor adventure dog or live somewhere hot

picks.description: The Sussex Spaniel is a low-slung, golden-liver spaniel known for an easygoing, unhurried temperament. It has low energy for a sporting breed, so 30 to 45 minutes of walks a day is usually enough, and it rarely barks at home. Sussex Spaniels are gentle, loyal and good with children and other pets. The long, wavy coat sheds moderately and needs brushing a few times a week, plus ear cleaning. They can be slow to train and may bay when they pick up a scent outdoors. The breed is rare, so expect a breeder waitlist.
picks.best_for: Calm households wanting a relaxed, medium-sized companion
picks.quirky_fact: Sussex Spaniels have a rolling gait that sets them apart from other spaniels.
picks.skip_if: You want a quick learner or an easy-to-find breed

picks.description: The Clumber Spaniel is the heaviest spaniel, 55 to 85 pounds, and one of the most laid-back sporting dogs. It needs moderate daily walks and rarely barks. Clumbers are gentle, loyal and good with children and other pets. The dense white coat sheds moderately to heavily and needs brushing a few times a week, and the breed drools and snores. Their size and weight mean they need room and should avoid too much jumping as puppies. A good fit for people who want a big, mellow, quiet dog without giant-breed size.
picks.best_for: People wanting a large, quiet, mellow dog without giant size
picks.quirky_fact: Clumber Spaniels are named after Clumber Park, a former estate in Nottinghamshire, England.
picks.skip_if: You dislike drool, snoring or white hair on dark clothes

picks.description: The Maltese is a gentle toy dog of under 7 pounds with low energy needs and an easy-to-train nature. It is affectionate, playful and good with children and other pets, though its size makes rough play risky. The long, silky white coat sheds little but needs daily brushing or a short puppy clip with regular grooming, plus cleaning around the eyes to prevent tear stains. Maltese can bark at noises, so early training on a quiet cue helps. They want company and dislike long hours alone.
picks.best_for: Calm adults wanting a tiny, low-shedding, affectionate dog
picks.quirky_fact: The Maltese has been a companion dog for over two thousand years.
picks.skip_if: You have rough toddlers or won't keep up with grooming

picks.description: The Shih Tzu is a calm, affectionate small dog with low exercise needs, around 20 to 30 minutes a day. It is friendly with children and other pets and adapts well to apartments. The long, silky coat sheds little but tangles quickly, so brush daily or keep a short clip with regular grooming. Shih Tzus can be stubborn about house-training and may bark at the door. Their short muzzle makes them sensitive to heat, and their eyes need regular cleaning.
picks.best_for: Apartment dwellers wanting a calm, low-shedding lap dog
picks.quirky_fact: Shih Tzus were bred as palace companions in imperial China.
picks.skip_if: You want a fast learner or live somewhere very hot

picks.description: The Bulldog is a calm, low-energy medium dog that is happy with short walks and long naps, and it rarely barks. It is affectionate and gentle with children and other pets. The short coat needs a weekly brush, but facial folds need daily cleaning. The trade-offs are health and noise of another kind: Bulldogs snore, can drool, overheat easily and are prone to breathing, skin and joint problems, so vet costs are higher than average. Lifespan is around 8 to 10 years. Choose a breeder who prioritizes health.
picks.best_for: Relaxed owners wanting a gentle, quiet, low-energy dog
picks.quirky_fact: Bulldogs often can't swim because of their heavy chests, so pools need supervision.
picks.skip_if: You can't budget for vet care or live somewhere hot

picks.description: The Mastiff is a giant, gentle, low-energy dog that often weighs 120 pounds or more and rarely barks. It is calm indoors, good with children, cats and other dogs when raised with them, and naturally protective. Daily walks of moderate length are enough. The short coat is easy to groom but sheds, and Mastiffs drool. Their size means a big home, a big car and big bills for food and vet care. Lifespan is short, around 6 to 10 years. Training should start early, since a full-grown Mastiff is too strong to manage by force.
picks.best_for: Calm households with space wanting a quiet, gentle guardian
picks.quirky_fact: Mastiffs are among the heaviest dog breeds, with some males exceeding 200 pounds.
picks.skip_if: You live in a small space or mind drool and short lifespans

picks.description: The Saint Bernard is a giant, gentle, low-energy dog that rarely barks and is famously patient with children. It gets along with cats and other dogs. Daily walks are enough, though Saints dislike heat and prefer cool climates. Coats come short or long; both shed heavily, and Saints drool a lot. They need a lot of space and a budget for giant-breed food and vet care. Lifespan is around 8 to 10 years. Early training matters because adults are very strong.
picks.best_for: Families in cool climates wanting a patient, quiet giant
picks.quirky_fact: Saint Bernards were bred by monks in the Swiss Alps to help find travelers in snow.
picks.skip_if: You live somewhere hot or can't handle heavy drool and shedding

picks.description: The Tibetan Spaniel is a small, calm companion breed of 9 to 15 pounds with low exercise needs. It is affectionate with its family, good with children and other pets, and somewhat independent, often perching on furniture to watch the room. Tibbies bark to alert, so they are not silent, but they are not usually nuisance barkers. The medium-long coat sheds moderately and needs brushing once or twice a week. They can be aloof with strangers and moderately stubborn to train.
picks.best_for: Quiet homes wanting a small, independent, watchful companion
picks.quirky_fact: Tibetan Spaniels were kept in monasteries, where they reportedly sat on walls as lookouts.
picks.skip_if: You want a dog that is instantly friendly with every visitor

picks.description: The Basset Hound is low-energy and easygoing indoors, gentle and friendly with children and other pets. It needs daily walks to stay lean, since Bassets gain weight easily and their long backs suffer from extra pounds. The short coat sheds moderately and needs little grooming, but the long ears need regular cleaning. The big trade-off for a quiet home is voice: Bassets bay loudly, especially when bored or on a scent. They are also hard to train and will follow their nose.
picks.best_for: Relaxed homes with a yard that don't mind an occasional howl
picks.quirky_fact: A Basset's long ears help sweep scent toward its nose while tracking.
picks.skip_if: You live in an apartment with thin walls or want an obedient dog

picks.description: The Lhasa Apso is a small, calm dog bred as a sentinel in Tibetan monasteries. It has low exercise needs and is loyal and affectionate with its family, though independent and wary of strangers. Lhasas will bark to alert. The long coat needs daily brushing or a short clip with regular grooming. They are hard to train, so patience and short, positive sessions matter. A good fit for calm adults who want a small dog with a dignified, self-assured personality.
picks.best_for: Calm adults wanting a small, independent, loyal dog
picks.quirky_fact: Lhasa Apsos were traditionally given as gifts rather than sold.
picks.skip_if: You want an easy-to-train dog or minimal grooming

picks.description: The Dogue de Bordeaux is a massive French mastiff, calm and low-energy indoors and deeply loyal to its family. It needs moderate daily walks. The short coat is easy to groom but sheds, and the breed drools heavily. Dogues are protective and need early socialization and confident training. The dataset flags them as not good with cats. Their lifespan is the shortest on this list, around 5 to 8 years, which is the biggest consideration for most families.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners wanting a calm, loyal guardian breed
picks.quirky_fact: The Dogue de Bordeaux has one of the largest heads relative to body size of any dog breed.
picks.skip_if: You have cats or want a long-lived dog

picks.description: The Neapolitan Mastiff is a giant, wrinkled guardian breed that is calm and low-energy at home but intensely protective. It needs moderate walks and plenty of space. The short coat is easy to groom, but the wrinkles need cleaning and the breed drools heavily. Neapolitans are hard to train and need an experienced owner and early socialization. The dataset flags them as not good with cats or other dogs, so they suit single-pet homes. Lifespan is around 7 to 9 years.
picks.best_for: Experienced owners wanting a calm, imposing single-pet guardian
picks.quirky_fact: Neapolitan Mastiffs were developed in southern Italy as estate and property guardians.
picks.skip_if: You have other pets, little experience, or limited space

faqs.question: What is the calmest dog breed?
faqs.answer: Among common breeds, the Japanese Chin, Bulldog, Basset Hound, Mastiff and Shih Tzu are known for low energy. For a calm dog that is also quiet, the Japanese Chin and the Sussex and Clumber Spaniels stand out. Individual temperament varies, so meet the dog first.

faqs.question: What is the calmest small dog breed?
faqs.answer: The Japanese Chin, Shih Tzu and Maltese are calm small breeds with low exercise needs. The Chin is especially quiet. All three are affectionate lap dogs, though the Shih Tzu and Maltese need regular grooming.

faqs.question: What is the best calm dog for an apartment?
faqs.answer: Small, low-barking breeds suit apartments best, especially the Japanese Chin, Shih Tzu and Maltese. The Bulldog is a calm medium option that snores but rarely barks. Giant calm breeds like Mastiffs need more space than most apartments offer.

faqs.question: Do calm dogs still need exercise?
faqs.answer: Yes. Even low-energy breeds need daily walks to stay at a healthy weight and avoid boredom. Many calm breeds are prone to weight gain, so 20 to 45 minutes of gentle activity a day and measured meals matter.

faqs.question: Which calm dog breeds don't bark much?
faqs.answer: The Japanese Chin, Sussex Spaniel, Clumber Spaniel, Bulldog, Mastiff and Saint Bernard are all rated low for barking. Hounds like the Basset are calm but may howl or bay, which carries further than a bark.

seo_title: 13 Calm Dog Breeds for Quiet Homes (2026)
answer: The Japanese Chin, Sussex Spaniel and Clumber Spaniel are the calmest, quietest fits for a peaceful home: low energy, rarely barking, and gentle with children and other pets. If you want a small lap dog, choose the Chin, Maltese or Shih Tzu; if you want a big, mellow dog and have the space, the Mastiff or Saint Bernard.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for low-energy breeds, then ordered them by barking level and by how well each gets along with children, cats and other dogs, putting the quietest and most adaptable first.
author: Elena Marsh
